claim: Anorexia nervosa has among the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder.
source: Anorexia nervosa has among the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder and is characterized by cognitive inflexibility that persists after weight recovery and contributes to the chronic nature of the condition.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence, though it represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by cognitive inflexibility that persists after weight recovery.
source: Anorexia nervosa has among the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder and is characterized by cognitive inflexibility that persists after weight recovery and contributes to the chronic nature of the condition.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract representing established knowledge about anorexia nervosa.

claim: Cognitive inflexibility contributes to the chronic nature of anorexia nervosa.
source: Anorexia nervosa has among the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder and is characterized by cognitive inflexibility that persists after weight recovery and contributes to the chronic nature of the condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of cognitive inflexibility in anorexia nervosa based on established understanding.

claim: Previous work identified a neurobiological link between cognitive inflexibility and susceptibility to pathological weight loss in female rats using the ABA model.
source: Our previous work using the most well-established animal model of anorexia nervosa, known as activity-based anorexia (ABA) identified a neurobiological link between cognitive inflexibility and susceptibility to pathological weight loss in female rats.
evidence: This refers to prior published work by the authors.

claim: Testing flexible learning prior to ABA exposure in the same animals has been impossible due to the length of training required and the necessity of daily handling.
source: However, testing flexible learning prior to exposure to ABA in the same animals has been thus far impossible due to the length of training required and the necessity of daily handling, which can itself influence the development of ABA.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous experimental approaches.

claim: Daily handling can influence the development of ABA.
source: However, testing flexible learning prior to exposure to ABA in the same animals has been thus far impossible due to the length of training required and the necessity of daily handling, which can itself influence the development of ABA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation elsewhere in the manuscript (Carrera et al., 2006).

claim: The automated touchscreen testing system substantially reduces testing time compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods.
source: First, we show substantially reduced testing time and increased throughput compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods because animals engage in test sessions at their own direction and can complete multiple sessions per day without experimenter involvement.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The automated touchscreen testing system increases throughput compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods.
source: First, we show substantially reduced testing time and increased throughput compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods because animals engage in test sessions at their own direction and can complete multiple sessions per day without experimenter involvement.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Animals can complete multiple sessions per day without experimenter involvement in the automated system.
source: First, we show substantially reduced testing time and increased throughput compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods because animals engage in test sessions at their own direction and can complete multiple sessions per day without experimenter involvement.
evidence: This describes a feature of the automated system demonstrated in the study.

claim: Cognitive inflexibility measured by reversal learning does not predispose rats to pathological weight loss in ABA.
source: We also show that, contrary to expectations, cognitive inflexibility measured by this reversal learning task does not predispose rats to pathological weight loss in ABA.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Rats predisposed to weight loss in ABA were more quickly able to learn the reversal task prior to ABA exposure.
source: Instead, rats that were predisposed to weight loss in ABA were more quickly able to learn this reversal task prior to ABA exposure.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: ABA-exposed but weight-recovered rats perform much worse than ABA naïve rats on the reversal learning task.
source: Intriguingly, we show reciprocal links between ABA exposure and cognitive flexibility, with ABA-exposed (but weight-recovered) rats performing much worse than ABA naïve rats on the reversal learning task, an impairment that did not occur to the same extent in rats exposed to food restriction conditions alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The impairment in reversal learning after ABA exposure did not occur to the same extent in rats exposed to food restriction conditions alone.
source: Intriguingly, we show reciprocal links between ABA exposure and cognitive flexibility, with ABA-exposed (but weight-recovered) rats performing much worse than ABA naïve rats on the reversal learning task, an impairment that did not occur to the same extent in rats exposed to food restriction conditions alone.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data comparing ABA-exposed and food restriction-only groups.

claim: Animals that had been trained on reversal learning were better able to resist weight loss upon subsequent exposure to the ABA model.
source: On the other hand, animals that had been trained on reversal learning were better able to resist weight loss upon subsequent exposure to the ABA model.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Machine learning tools uncovered stable behavioral differences between ABA susceptible versus resistant rats during touchscreen test sessions.
source: We also uncovered some stable behavioral differences between ABA susceptible versus resistant rats during touchscreen test sessions using machine learning tools that highlight possible predictors of anorectic phenotypes.
evidence: This is a finding supported by DeepLabCut and B-SOiD analysis presented in supplementary figures.

claim: Cognitive flexibility refers to the capacity to modify behavioral choices to meet the demands of a changing environment.
source: Cognitive flexibility refers to the capacity to modify behavioral choices to meet the demands of a changing environment and is crucial for selecting appropriate responses based on context and circumstance (Diamond, 2013).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Diamond, 2013.

claim: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to schizophrenia.
source: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to a range of psychiatric illnesses including schizophrenia (Floresco et al., 2009; Thai et al., 2019), obsessive-compulsive disorder (Gruner and Pittenger, 2017), and substance use disorders (Smith and Laiks, 2018; Sampedro-Piquero et al., 2019), which are characterized by stereotypical patterns of rigid behaviors that persist despite negative consequences, ultimately impacting decision-making.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Floresco et al., 2009 and Thai et al., 2019.

claim: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to obsessive-compulsive disorder.
source: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to a range of psychiatric illnesses including schizophrenia (Floresco et al., 2009; Thai et al., 2019), obsessive-compulsive disorder (Gruner and Pittenger, 2017), and substance use disorders (Smith and Laiks, 2018; Sampedro-Piquero et al., 2019), which are characterized by stereotypical patterns of rigid behaviors that persist despite negative consequences, ultimately impacting decision-making.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gruner and Pittenger, 2017.

claim: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to substance use disorders.
source: Impairments in cognitive flexibility are common to a range of psychiatric illnesses including schizophrenia (Floresco et al., 2009; Thai et al., 2019), obsessive-compulsive disorder (Gruner and Pittenger, 2017), and substance use disorders (Smith and Laiks, 2018; Sampedro-Piquero et al., 2019), which are characterized by stereotypical patterns of rigid behaviors that persist despite negative consequences, ultimately impacting decision-making.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith and Laiks, 2018 and Sampedro-Piquero et al., 2019.

claim: Individuals with current or previous diagnosis of anorexia nervosa exhibit rigid behaviors, especially surrounding illness-relevant stimuli such as feeding and exercise.
source: Individuals with a current or previous diagnosis of anorexia nervosa also exhibit rigid behaviors, especially surrounding illness-relevant stimuli such as feeding and exercise (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Tchanturia et al., 2004; Galimberti et al., 2013; Roberts et al., 2010; Steinglass et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in patients acutely ill with anorexia nervosa.
source: While impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in patients acutely ill with anorexia nervosa and likely contributes to perpetuating the condition (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2010), the persistence of inflexible behavior following weight recovery and in unaffected sisters of patients with anorexia nervosa suggests that it is involved in the etiology of the disorder (Roberts et al., 2010; Steinglass et al., 2006; Tenconi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tchanturia et al., 2012 and Roberts et al., 2010.

claim: Impaired cognitive flexibility likely contributes to perpetuating anorexia nervosa.
source: While impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in patients acutely ill with anorexia nervosa and likely contributes to perpetuating the condition (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2010), the persistence of inflexible behavior following weight recovery and in unaffected sisters of patients with anorexia nervosa suggests that it is involved in the etiology of the disorder (Roberts et al., 2010; Steinglass et al., 2006; Tenconi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference from clinical observations.

claim: The persistence of inflexible behavior following weight recovery in patients with anorexia nervosa suggests it is involved in the etiology of the disorder.
source: While impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in patients acutely ill with anorexia nervosa and likely contributes to perpetuating the condition (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2010), the persistence of inflexible behavior following weight recovery and in unaffected sisters of patients with anorexia nervosa suggests that it is involved in the etiology of the disorder (Roberts et al., 2010; Steinglass et al., 2006; Tenconi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Inflexible behavior is present in unaffected sisters of patients with anorexia nervosa.
source: While impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in patients acutely ill with anorexia nervosa and likely contributes to perpetuating the condition (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2010), the persistence of inflexible behavior following weight recovery and in unaffected sisters of patients with anorexia nervosa suggests that it is involved in the etiology of the disorder (Roberts et al., 2010; Steinglass et al., 2006; Tenconi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Studies assessing cognitive flexibility in patient populations are prone to inconsistent findings.
source: While the premise that cognitive rigidity is a fundamental trait of anorexia nervosa is well-accepted, studies assessing cognitive flexibility in patient populations are prone to inconsistent findings, which are likely amplified by large discrepancies in participant demographics and experimental approaches (Miles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miles et al., 2020.

claim: Inconsistent findings in cognitive flexibility studies are likely amplified by large discrepancies in participant demographics and experimental approaches.
source: While the premise that cognitive rigidity is a fundamental trait of anorexia nervosa is well-accepted, studies assessing cognitive flexibility in patient populations are prone to inconsistent findings, which are likely amplified by large discrepancies in participant demographics and experimental approaches (Miles et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Miles et al., 2020.

claim: The ABA model has been instrumental in identifying specific neural circuits that contribute to disordered cognitive functioning.
source: Rodent models that incorporate key aetiological features, such as the most well-established animal model of anorexia nervosa known as ABA, have been instrumental in identifying the specific neural circuits that contribute to disordered cognitive functioning (Milton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: Touchscreen testing in rodents closely mimics those used for human cognitive testing.
source: A major contribution to improving translation has been the incorporation of touchscreens displaying visual stimuli in rodent test batteries that closely mimic those used for human cognitive testing (Bussey et al., 2008), which improves the standardization and interpretation of data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bussey et al., 2008.

claim: Touchscreen testing in rodents improves the standardization and interpretation of data.
source: A major contribution to improving translation has been the incorporation of touchscreens displaying visual stimuli in rodent test batteries that closely mimic those used for human cognitive testing (Bussey et al., 2008), which improves the standardization and interpretation of data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bussey et al., 2008.

claim: Touchscreen testing in rodents has required significant time and experimenter intervention to transfer subjects to and from the testing chamber.
source: However, touchscreen testing in rodents has thus far required significant time and experimenter intervention to transfer subjects to and from the testing chamber.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of conventional touchscreen testing based on established knowledge.

claim: Experimenter involvement influences experimental outcomes, particularly for behavioral studies.
source: Indeed, it is well known that experimenter involvement influences experimental outcomes, particularly so for behavioral studies - including those involving the ABA model, in which the outcomes are known to be influenced by experimenter handling (Carrera et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carrera et al., 2006.

claim: ABA outcomes are influenced by experimenter handling.
source: Indeed, it is well known that experimenter involvement influences experimental outcomes, particularly so for behavioral studies - including those involving the ABA model, in which the outcomes are known to be influenced by experimenter handling (Carrera et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carrera et al., 2006.

claim: Stress from handling varies between experimenters and differentially impacts task performance.
source: Along with stress from handling, which varies between experimenters and, therefore, differentially impacts upon task performance (Deutsch-Feldman et al., 2015; Sorge et al., 2014; Meijer et al., 2007), manual transfer to test chambers at times that suit the experimenter is insensitive to the current motivational state of the animal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deutsch-Feldman et al., 2015; Sorge et al., 2014; Meijer et al., 2007.

claim: Social isolation can induce cognitive deficits.
source: Considering that social isolation itself can induce cognitive deficits (Bianchi et al., 2006; Hemmer et al., 2019) and depression-like behavior (Ieraci et al., 2016; Fone and Porkess, 2008), this is a huge confound for the assessment of cognition in rodent models.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bianchi et al., 2006 and Hemmer et al., 2019.

claim: Social isolation can induce depression-like behavior.
source: Considering that social isolation itself can induce cognitive deficits (Bianchi et al., 2006; Hemmer et al., 2019) and depression-like behavior (Ieraci et al., 2016; Fone and Porkess, 2008), this is a huge confound for the assessment of cognition in rodent models.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ieraci et al., 2016 and Fone and Porkess, 2008.

claim: Appropriate social interaction can enhance neuroplasticity.
source: In contrast, appropriate social interaction can enhance neuroplasticity (Liang et al., 2019), emotional and social intelligence (Torquet et al., 2018) and influence performance on complex cognitive tasks (Nagy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2019.

claim: Social interaction can enhance emotional and social intelligence.
source: In contrast, appropriate social interaction can enhance neuroplasticity (Liang et al., 2019), emotional and social intelligence (Torquet et al., 2018) and influence performance on complex cognitive tasks (Nagy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torquet et al., 2018.

claim: Social interaction can influence performance on complex cognitive tasks.
source: In contrast, appropriate social interaction can enhance neuroplasticity (Liang et al., 2019), emotional and social intelligence (Torquet et al., 2018) and influence performance on complex cognitive tasks (Nagy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nagy et al., 2020.

claim: The learning rate of self-motivated and undisturbed rats was much faster when experimenter involvement is removed.
source: This study demonstrated that the learning rate of self-motivated and undisturbed rats was much faster when experimenter involvement is removed.
evidence: This refers to findings from Rivalan et al., 2017 study.

claim: The ABA model develops differently in adult compared to adolescent ages.
source: The potential to more rapidly test cognition in rodents without experimenter intervention and in social groups opens the door to examine whether cognitive inflexibility predisposes individuals to pathological weight loss in ABA – particularly important because the ABA model develops differently in adult compared to adolescent ages (Beeler and Burghardt, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beeler and Burghardt, 2021.

claim: Young female rats were used because they are particularly vulnerable to developing the ABA phenotype.
source: Young female rats were used in these studies because they are particularly vulnerable to developing the ABA phenotype, a feature that is incompletely understood but has translational relevance to the increased prevalence of anorexia nervosa in young women.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for using young female rats based on established knowledge.

claim: The vulnerability of young female rats to ABA has translational relevance to the increased prevalence of anorexia nervosa in young women.
source: Young female rats were used in these studies because they are particularly vulnerable to developing the ABA phenotype, a feature that is incompletely understood but has translational relevance to the increased prevalence of anorexia nervosa in young women.
evidence: This is an inference about the translational relevance of the model.

claim: A male rat was housed in experimental rooms to facilitate synchronization of cycling in female rats (Whitten Effect).
source: Because both wheel running and food intake are known to fluctuate with the estrous cycle in female rats (Anantharaman-Barr and Decombaz, 1989), a male rat was housed in all experimental rooms at least 7 days prior to experimentation in order to facilitate synchronization of cycling, known as the Whitten Effect (Cora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by citations to Anantharaman-Barr and Decombaz, 1989 and Cora et al., 2015.

claim: Wheel running and food intake fluctuate with the estrous cycle in female rats.
source: Because both wheel running and food intake are known to fluctuate with the estrous cycle in female rats (Anantharaman-Barr and Decombaz, 1989), a male rat was housed in all experimental rooms at least 7 days prior to experimentation in order to facilitate synchronization of cycling, known as the Whitten Effect (Cora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anantharaman-Barr and Decombaz, 1989.

claim: The automated touchscreen testing system reduces the number of testing days to reach reversal learning performance criterion by up to 10 times compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods.
source: We demonstrated that the automated system reduces the number of testing days to reach the reversal learning performance criterion by up to 10 times compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods (i.e. Milton et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2A and comparison to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: Subsequent reversals were progressively easier to learn than the initial reversal with fewer sessions required to reach the performance criterion.
source: We also confirmed that subsequent reversals were progressively easier to learn than the initial reversal with fewer sessions required to reach the performance criterion (first reversal > second reversal: p=0.0099; first reversal > third reversal: p=0.0070; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 2B.

claim: The speed of learning serial reversals was driven largely by reduced omissions at the second and third reversals.
source: Interestingly, the speed of learning serial reversals was driven largely by reduced omissions at the second and third reversals (all ps <0.0309; Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 2D-E.

claim: Restricting touchscreen access to the dark phase increased accuracy overall.
source: Restricting access to the dark phase increased accuracy overall (p=0.0039; Figure 2G) and especially in pairwise discrimination (p=0.0371), which was specific for initial learning, whereby more substantial between-group differences were seen during the first 100 trials (p=0.0030; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 2G.

claim: Dark-phase restriction reduced the number of omitted responses during both pairwise discrimination and reversal.
source: Dark-phase restriction also reduced the number of omitted responses during both pairwise discrimination and reversal (Figure 2I), however, this was not significantly different overall (p=0.0737; Figure 2J) but rather restricted to the initial stages of discrimination and reversal learning (pairwise discrimination p=0.0024; reversal p=0.0332; Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 2I-K.

claim: 55% of rats exposed to ABA conditions were able to maintain body weight above 80% of baseline throughout the 10 days of ABA, being classified as 'resistant'.
source: Our previous ABA studies demonstrate that rats segregate into susceptible and resistant subpopulations and in the present study, 12/22 (55%) rats exposed to ABA conditions were able to maintain body weight above 80% of baseline throughout the 10 days of ABA, therefore being classified as 'resistant.'
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data.

claim: Rats that went on to be susceptible to ABA were able to learn pairwise discrimination at the same rate as rats that went on to be resistant to ABA.
source: Rats that went on to be susceptible to ABA were able to learn pairwise discrimination at the same rate as rats that went on to be resistant to ABA, as demonstrated by a similar number of sessions and trials to reach the performance criterion (all ps>0.8214; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Rats that went on to be resistant to ABA required significantly more sessions at the first reversal to reach the performance criterion.
source: Interestingly, rats that went on to be resistant to weight loss in ABA required significantly more sessions at the first reversal to reach the performance criterion (p=0.0142; Figure 3B), and although this did not translate to a significant increase in overall trials required (p=0.1132; Figure 3C) it related specifically to an increase in non-correct responses (i.e. incorrect + omitted responses, p=0.0401; Figure 3E), a finding that was reinforced by examining learning rate in the early perseverative phase of reversal (first 100 trials; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 3B, 3C, 3E, and 3F.

claim: During initial discrimination learning, rats that went on to be resistant to ABA spent more time engaged in vertical exploration (rearing) compared to susceptible rats.
source: Analysis of behavioral profiles during touchscreen testing sessions revealed that during initial discrimination learning, rats that went on to be resistant to ABA spent more time engaged in vertical exploration (rearing; p=0.0336) and locomoting (p=0.0190) compared to susceptible rats, which were significantly more inactive (p<0.0001) during touchscreen testing sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from machine learning analysis of behavior supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Rats that went on to be susceptible to ABA were significantly more inactive during touchscreen testing sessions.
source: Analysis of behavioral profiles during touchscreen testing sessions revealed that during initial discrimination learning, rats that went on to be resistant to ABA spent more time engaged in vertical exploration (rearing; p=0.0336) and locomoting (p=0.0190) compared to susceptible rats, which were significantly more inactive (p<0.0001) during touchscreen testing sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from machine learning analysis of behavior supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Half (50%) of ABA-exposed animals were unable to acquire the reversal learning task.
source: Not only were half (50%) of ABA-exposed animals unable to acquire the reversal learning task, compared to 32% of animals exposed to restricted food access and 11% of ABA-naïve animals (Figure 4B), task acquisition was significantly slower than ABA-naïve rats.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: 32% of animals exposed to restricted food access were unable to acquire the reversal learning task.
source: Not only were half (50%) of ABA-exposed animals unable to acquire the reversal learning task, compared to 32% of animals exposed to restricted food access and 11% of ABA-naïve animals (Figure 4B), task acquisition was significantly slower than ABA-naïve rats.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: 11% of ABA-naïve animals were unable to acquire the reversal learning task.
source: Not only were half (50%) of ABA-exposed animals unable to acquire the reversal learning task, compared to 32% of animals exposed to restricted food access and 11% of ABA-naïve animals (Figure 4B), task acquisition was significantly slower than ABA-naïve rats.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Exposure to ABA conditions increased the number of sessions required to reach performance criteria compared to ABA-naïve animals.
source: Exposure to ABA conditions increased the number of sessions required to reach performance criteria compared to ABA-naïve animals (ABA exposure p=0.0051; pairwise discrimination p=0.0098; reversal p=0.0205) with a similar trend compared to food restriction-only animals (ABA exposure p=0.0858; pairwise discrimination p=0.0539; reversal p=0.3985; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of correct, incorrect, and omitted trials to the acquisition of initial discrimination were significantly greater in the ABA-exposed group.
source: While there was no overall difference in the number of trials required to reach progression criteria across the entirety of the experiment (p=0.1240; Figure 4D), the number of correct (versus ABA-naïve p=0.0185; versus food restriction-only p=0.0259), incorrect (versus food restriction-only p=0.0479) and omitted (versus ABA-naïve p=0.0224) trials to the acquisition of initial discrimination were significantly greater in the ABA-exposed group (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: During pairwise discrimination, ABA-exposed animals spent more time inactive and less time engaged in task-relevant behaviors like rotating, investigating, and magazine interactions than did ABA-naïve animals.
source: Video analysis of touchscreen sessions revealed that during pairwise discrimination, ABA-exposed animals spent more time inactive and less time engaged in task-relevant behaviors like rotating, investigating, and magazine interactions than did ABA-naïve animals, whereas behavioral profiles were more similar between groups for reversal sessions (see Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from machine learning analysis of behavior supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Significantly more rats that underwent cognitive testing prior to ABA were able to resist the precipitous weight loss that characterizes the model.
source: Significantly more rats that underwent cognitive testing prior to ABA were able to resist the precipitous weight loss that characterizes the model (p<0.0001; Figure 5B) and demonstrated a slow trajectory of body weight loss that plateaued over consecutive days of ABA exposure (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Rats that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA lost significantly less body weight each day.
source: When comparing outcomes for both susceptible and resistant animals on key ABA measures, those that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA lost significantly less body weight each day (p<0.0001; Figure 5D) and ate more food when food was available (p=0.0009; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Rats that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA ate more food when food was available.
source: When comparing outcomes for both susceptible and resistant animals on key ABA measures, those that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA lost significantly less body weight each day (p<0.0001; Figure 5D) and ate more food when food was available (p=0.0009; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 5E.

claim: Rats that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA showed a blunted hyperactive phenotype when ABA conditions commenced.
source: Rats that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA also showed a blunted hyperactive phenotype when ABA conditions commenced that was already evident under baseline conditions (p<0.0001; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 5F.

claim: Running activity overall was significantly reduced in animals that had previously undergone cognitive testing both at baseline and during ABA.
source: Although running activity overall was significantly reduced in animals that had previously undergone cognitive testing both at baseline and during ABA (overall p=0.0002; baseline p=0.0160; ABA p<0.0001; Figure 5G), these rats showed elevated running specifically in the hour preceding food access, known as food anticipatory activity, which is an adaptive response to scheduled feeding (overall p<0.0001; baseline p=0.0010; ABA p<0.0001; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Rats that had previously undergone cognitive testing showed elevated running specifically in the hour preceding food access (food anticipatory activity).
source: Although running activity overall was significantly reduced in animals that had previously undergone cognitive testing both at baseline and during ABA (overall p=0.0002; baseline p=0.0160; ABA p<0.0001; Figure 5G), these rats showed elevated running specifically in the hour preceding food access, known as food anticipatory activity, which is an adaptive response to scheduled feeding (overall p<0.0001; baseline p=0.0010; ABA p<0.0001; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and data in Figure 5H.

claim: Elevated food anticipatory activity is consistently associated with resistance to ABA.
source: While our previous work has shown elevated food anticipatory activity to be consistently associated with resistance to ABA (Milton et al., 2021; Milton et al., 2018; Milton et al., 2022), the increased food anticipatory activity at baseline for these animals suggests that an anticipatory response was carried over from the scheduled feeding conducted during touchscreen testing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Milton et al., 2021; Milton et al., 2018; Milton et al., 2022).

claim: The rate of learning in the automated system was five times faster than previously reported with conventional touchscreen testing.
source: Critically, the rate of learning in the automated system was shown to be five times faster (with approximately 10 times higher throughput) than previously reported with conventional touchscreen testing (Milton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding comparing the current study to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: The automated system provides approximately 10 times higher throughput than conventional touchscreen testing.
source: Critically, the rate of learning in the automated system was shown to be five times faster (with approximately 10 times higher throughput) than previously reported with conventional touchscreen testing (Milton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding comparing the current study to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: The number of omitted trials is reduced when touchscreen access was limited to the dark phase.
source: Our observation that the number of omitted trials is reduced (i.e. engagement is higher) when touchscreen access was limited to the dark phase is consistent with the well-established increase in activity (Milton et al., 2021) and attention (Bruinsma et al., 2019) that rats exhibit during the dark period.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by citations to Milton et al., 2021 and Bruinsma et al., 2019.

claim: Rats exhibit increased activity during the dark period.
source: Our observation that the number of omitted trials is reduced (i.e. engagement is higher) when touchscreen access was limited to the dark phase is consistent with the well-established increase in activity (Milton et al., 2021) and attention (Bruinsma et al., 2019) that rats exhibit during the dark period.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: Rats exhibit increased attention during the dark period.
source: Our observation that the number of omitted trials is reduced (i.e. engagement is higher) when touchscreen access was limited to the dark phase is consistent with the well-established increase in activity (Milton et al., 2021) and attention (Bruinsma et al., 2019) that rats exhibit during the dark period.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bruinsma et al., 2019.

claim: Previous work demonstrated that activity within a specific neural circuit (extending from the medial prefrontal cortex to the nucleus accumbens shell) links pathological weight loss in ABA with cognitive inflexibility on reversal learning.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that activity within a specific neural circuit (extending from the medial prefrontal cortex to the nucleus accumbens shell) links pathological weight loss in ABA with cognitive inflexibility on this reversal learning task (Milton et al., 2021) and suggested that inflexibility might be a biomarker for predicting susceptibility to ABA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Milton et al., 2021.

claim: Inflexibility does not predispose animals to the ABA phenotype.
source: The results presented here demonstrate that, contrary to our hypothesis, inflexibility does not predispose animals to the ABA phenotype but instead shows that rats that went on to be resistant to ABA were slower to learn the reversal task (i.e. were less flexible) than ABA-susceptible rats.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Rats that went on to be resistant to ABA were slower to learn the reversal task than ABA-susceptible rats.
source: The results presented here demonstrate that, contrary to our hypothesis, inflexibility does not predispose animals to the ABA phenotype but instead shows that rats that went on to be resistant to ABA were slower to learn the reversal task (i.e. were less flexible) than ABA-susceptible rats.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Exposure to ABA conditions, but not food restriction alone, significantly impairs cognitive flexibility.
source: Exposure to ABA conditions, but not food restriction alone, significantly impairs cognitive flexibility, indicating that the excessive exercise component of the ABA model disrupts the integration of new and existing learning that is necessary for performance on the reversal learning task.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A loss of behavioral flexibility following disrupted cholinergic activity in the dorsal striatum was associated with both facilitated habit formation and increased vulnerability to maladaptive eating in ABA mice.
source: A recent study in ABA mice demonstrated that a loss of behavioral flexibility following disrupted cholinergic activity in the dorsal striatum was associated with both facilitated habit formation and increased vulnerability to maladaptive eating (Favier et al., 2020) but neither the accelerated formation of habits, or inflexible behaviors were associated with changes in hyperactivity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Favier et al., 2020.

claim: Only a subset of patients suffering from anorexia nervosa show enhanced habit formation.
source: Recent evidence suggests that only a subset of patients suffering from anorexia nervosa show enhanced habit formation (Favier et al., 2020), which can be differentiated from a more goal-directed patient subgroup by decreased medial orbitofrontal cortex activation during reward anticipation (Steding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Favier et al., 2020 and Steding et al., 2019.

claim: Operant training prior to exposure to ABA alters the subsequent development of anorectic phenotypes, particularly by reducing the maladaptive wheel running that typifies the ABA model.
source: Our data also suggest that operant training prior to exposure to ABA also alters the subsequent development of anorectic phenotypes, particularly by reducing the maladaptive wheel running that typifies the ABA model.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The cohort of rats that were experimentally naïve prior to ABA exposure was surprisingly mostly susceptible to weight loss (21/22 rats).
source: It should also be noted that the cohort of rats that were experimentally naïve prior to ABA exposure was surprisingly mostly susceptible to weight loss (21/22 rats), a much higher proportion than is normally seen on a cohort-to-cohort basis.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data.

claim: Rats exposed to ABA subsequently showed marked impairments in both discrimination and reversal learning, even after body weight recovery.
source: While the identification of a behavioral predictor (or biomarker) for pathological weight loss in ABA remains a challenge, the finding that rats exposed to ABA subsequently showed marked impairments in both discrimination and reversal learning, even after body weight recovery, is entirely in line with the clinical presentation of inflexibility in patients with anorexia nervosa long after body weight recovery (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Friederich and Herzog, 2011; Tchanturia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to clinical literature.

claim: The clinical presentation of inflexibility in patients with anorexia nervosa persists long after body weight recovery.
source: While the identification of a behavioral predictor (or biomarker) for pathological weight loss in ABA remains a challenge, the finding that rats exposed to ABA subsequently showed marked impairments in both discrimination and reversal learning, even after body weight recovery, is entirely in line with the clinical presentation of inflexibility in patients with anorexia nervosa long after body weight recovery (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Friederich and Herzog, 2011; Tchanturia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tchanturia et al., 2012; Friederich and Herzog, 2011; Tchanturia et al., 2004.

evidence: This is a finding supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The present study's finding contrasts with the only other published report of flexible learning after exposure to ABA, in which reversal learning was impaired at low body weight in ABA rats but ameliorated with weight recovery.
source: Our finding is in contrast to the only other published report of flexible learning after exposure to ABA (Allen et al., 2017), in which reversal learning was impaired at low body weight in ABA rats but ameliorated with weight recovery.
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from Allen et al., 2017.

claim: Impairments following ABA were observed not only on flexible updating of operant responses but also initial discrimination learning, pointing to a potential motivational deficit induced by ABA.
source: That we observed impairments following ABA not only on flexible updating of operant responses but also initial discrimination learning points to a potential motivational deficit induced by ABA.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that ABA impairs both reversal and discrimination learning.

claim: Previous work demonstrated a role for the mesolimbic dopamine circuitry in the development and maintenance of the ABA phenotype.
source: This is in line with our previous work demonstrating a role for the mesolimbic dopamine circuitry in the development and maintenance of the ABA phenotype (Foldi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foldi et al., 2017.

claim: Exercise behavior in anorexia nervosa is linked with dopaminergic activity.
source: Considering that exercise behavior in anorexia nervosa is also linked with dopaminergic activity (Gorrell et al., 2020), future studies should define the time course over which motivation or reward-based deficits arise during ABA and the specific influence of ABA on dopamine signaling in response to reward anticipation and receipt using in vivo fiber photometric recordings paired with detection of dopamine release (using the GRAB_DA sensor; Sun et al., 2018) or dopamine binding (using the dLight sensor Patriarchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gorrell et al., 2020.

claim: The application of DeepLabCut and B-SOiD to the prediction of behaviors allowed for additional exploration of behaviors that could contribute toward cognitive task performance in rats.
source: The application of DeepLabCut and B-SOiD to the prediction of behaviors in the present study has allowed for additional exploration of behaviors that could contribute toward cognitive task performance in rats that will aid in the generation of hypotheses to be tested in future studies.
evidence: This describes the utility of machine learning tools used in the study.

claim: Using DeepLabCut and B-SOiD enabled the scoring of very large datasets, such as the 185 hr of footage analyzed in this study.
source: Using these tools also enabled the scoring of very large datasets, such as the 185 hr of footage analyzed here.
evidence: This describes the capability of the machine learning tools used in the study.
